query: Earlier studies used carbothermal shock, fast moving-bed pyrolysis, microwave heating, polyol synthesis, and dealloying, but a straightforward, cost-effective, and scalable route remains unavailable. Prior comparative work produced sharply different outcomes among multimetal nanoparticle systems—including homogeneous alloy formation versus phase separation, elemental segregation, uncontrolled morphology, and high decomposition temperatures—without establishing a general cause. The challenge increases with more than five interacting elements and the requirement to preserve substantial surface-atom exposure for catalytic applications. Against this background, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis explains what governs successful formation of noble metal–based high-entropy alloy nanoparticles and why? Describe one controlled comparison without naming the variable or investigative technique, predict the observations relative to an unchanged baseline, define where the hypothesis should and should not apply, relate it to the reported comparative evidence, and identify a decisive falsifying result.

generation.hypothesis: The formation of single-phase noble metal-based high-entropy alloy nanoparticles is favored by the combination of multiple elements with similar chemical nature, which minimizes mixing enthalpies and promotes homogeneous mixing at the local level of the crystalline precursor.
generation.material_initial_state: Crystalline single-source precursor comprised of coordination compounds of anionic and cationic complexes
generation.intervention: Thermolysis in an H2-containing gas stream
generation.structural_mediator: Homogeneous mixing of elements at the local level of the crystalline precursor
generation.mechanism: Minimization of mixing enthalpies, promotion of single-phase formation
generation.predicted_outcome: Formation of single-phase HEA nanoparticles with improved electrocatalytic performance
generation.baseline: Phase separation, intermetallic phase formation, or uncontrolled morphology
generation.boundary: Limited to noble metal-based systems with similar chemical nature, may not apply to systems with large differences in chemical properties
generation.uncertainty: The exact role of entropy in stabilizing multi-metallic phases at low temperatures, the influence of synthesis parameters on phase formation

falsification_experiment.design: Comparison of single-phase formation in HEA nanoparticles synthesized with different combinations of noble metals, varying the number of elements and their chemical similarity
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the combination of multiple elements with similar chemical nature does not favor single-phase formation, or if the synthesis of HEA nanoparticles with large differences in chemical properties results in single-phase formation, the hypothesis is falsified.

Combined experimental and theoretical studies that utilize the predictions from computational screenings are still scarce and mainly focus on thin film catalyst materials prepared by magnetron sputtering that can be more easily performed in experimental high throughput screening studies. To be able to predict and simulate the variety of binding sites of the different elements present in a HEA, single-phase materials are crucial. If phase segregation occurs, the surface atoms are not randomly distributed anymore and the key assumption of the computational modeling is not valid. Thus the experimental and computational trends will diverge.
HEAs are conventionally prepared as bulk materials employing high-temperature methods such as arc melting. Bulk materials have very low dispersion, i.e., a low ratio of surface to bulk atoms. A large surface-to-bulk atom ratio is, however, vital for efficient catalysts. Nanoparticles possess such high dispersion. This generates a large interest in developing HEA nanoparticle synthesis methods. Many synthesis methods for HEA nanoparticles are high-energy shock methods such as Joule-heating, microwave heating, laser-ablation, and fast-bed pyrolysis. R

reduction of all individual elements (Pt, Ir, Os, Rh, Ru) is followed alongside the crystallization of HEA nanoparticles. Comparing multimetallic precursor mixtures with bimetallic ones, we propose a model for the formation of single-phase nanoparticles. The essential conclusion of the model, i.e., that combining multiple elements favors the formation of single-phase nanoparticles, will aid the design of future studies combining experimental investigations with computational simulations.
## Material synthesis
All samples were prepared following a literature procedure described by Yusenko et al. All compounds were prepared from commercial metal precursors (Sigma Aldrich). As cationic precursors the chloropentaammine metal chlorides of Ir, Rh, and Ru were used; Ir(NH3)5Cl]Cl2, [Rh(NH3)5Cl]Cl2, and [Ru(NH3)5Cl]Cl2. The anionic precursors were the ammonium hexachlorometallates of Ir, Pt, and Os; (NH4)2[IrCl6], (NH4)2[PtCl6], and (NH4)2[OsCl6]. In short, separate aqueous solutions of anionic metal precursors (hexachlorates) and cationic metal precursors (chloropentaamines) were prepared by dissolving the respective amounts of the individual metal salts in hot MilliQ water (90 °C). For ex situ characterization, alloy samples were prepared by thermal decomposition of the prepared crystalline single source-precursors in a reducing gas atmosphere (Carbagas, 5% H2 in Ar). The samples were calcined in a quartz-tube furnace (Gero SR-A 40-250/11) in quartz crucibles at 700 °C for 60 minutes (heating ramp 50 K min−1). The crystalline phases of the prepared samples were determined from powder X-ray diffraction (XRD) data using a STOE StadiP with a Cu Kα X-ray source in transmission geometry. The elemental composition was analyzed by energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDX) using a Zeiss Gemini 450 scanning electron microscope equipped with an Oxford Instruments UltimMax 65 EDX detector.
Synchrotron X-ray powder diffraction and X-ray total scattering data for pair distribution function (PDF) analysis of the prepared high entropy alloy samples was collected at DESY P21.1 at PETRAIII; DESY in Hamburg, Germany, with a wavelength of 0.12224 Å. All ex situ samples were prepared as powders in Kapton capillaries and data was collected at room temperature under a helium atmosphere to limit the background contribution arising from air scattering.

To obtain a qualitative measure of the mixing enthalpies of the bimetallic and HEA systems in both fcc and hcp crystal structures, the total energy of several bulk structures was calculated with density functional theory. The calculations used the revised Perdew–Burke–Ernzerhof (RPBE) exchange–correlation functional as implemented in the GPAW code. Each system was calculated as both fcc and hcp structures containing 32 and 16 atoms per cell, respectively. The elements of each atom in the binary systems were chosen randomly with equal probability and the elements in the HEA systems were chosen with probabilities corresponding to the precursor compositions: Ru0.11Rh0.26Os0.06Ir0.22Pt0.35 for the fcc-structure and Ru0.31Rh0.09Os0.30Ir0.15Pt0.15 for the hcp-structure. In all cases, the cell was scaled to the weighted mean of the lattice constants of the atoms constituting the cell. The wave functions were expanded in plane waves with an energy cut-off set to 600 eV, and the Brillouin zone was sampled with a Monkhorst–Pack grid of 4 × 4 × 4 and 8 × 8 × 4 k-points, for fcc and hcp structures respectively. 50 structures of each binary system were o

re under an Ar-gas stream humidified with IPA and H2O, leading to the catalyst films with a metal loading of 30 μgmetal cm−2 for the electrochemical measurements.
## In situ XRD/XAS studies
Combined XAS and XRD in situ experiments were performed at the BM31 beamline (SNBL) at the ESRF in Grenoble, France. Details on the in situ XRD/XAS studies can be found in the ESI,† see Fig. S1. Here, the beamline setup is presented and the data analysis is explained in depth. In short, a 0.7 mm quartz capillary fixed in a U-shaped stainless-steel bracket functioned as a miniature tube furnace. A gas stream of 5% H2 in He was flown through the capillary while heating to 500 °C with a constant heating ramp of 100 K h−1. XAS and XRD data were continuously collected during the heating.
## Results and discussion
As discussed in the introduction, the present study aims to investigate the drivers that favor the formation of single-phase HEA nanoparticles at low temperatures.
